qs.q: A patient taking low-dose aspirin for coronary artery disease develops recurrent gout flares. What is the appropriate management regarding their aspirin therapy?
o: It should be immediately replaced with systemic glucocorticoids
It should be discontinued until the intercritical stage is reached
It should be combined with high-dose probenecid to offset flares
It should not be stopped, despite decreasing uric acid excretion
qs.e: Although low-dose aspirin can decrease uric acid excretion and trigger flares, it should not be stopped in patients taking it for specific indications like coronary artery disease or cerebrovascular disease. Stopping it could jeopardize their cardiovascular health.

qs.q: In the medical management of NSTEMI or unstable angina, dual antiplatelet therapy typically combines aspirin with which class of medication?
o: A P2Y12 inhibitor
A beta-blocker agent
An aldosterone blocker
A loop diuretic agent
qs.e: Dual antiplatelet therapy for NSTEMI or unstable angina involves administering aspirin along with a P2Y12 inhibitor such as clopidogrel, ticagrelor, or prasugrel. Diuretics and beta-blockers serve different roles in symptom and rate control.

qs.q: What is the appropriate management strategy regarding low-dose aspirin in a patient who develops an acute gout flare while taking it for coronary artery disease?
o: Immediately discontinue aspirin regardless of cardiac indication
Double the aspirin dose to counteract the acute flare
Switch aspirin to high-dose ibuprofen treatment immediately
Do not stop aspirin despite its effect on uric acid
qs.e: Low-dose aspirin can decrease uric acid excretion and trigger flares, but it should not be stopped in patients taking it for specific indications like coronary artery disease or cerebrovascular disease. Stopping it could jeopardize their cardiovascular health.

qs.q: A patient with an acute gout flare is currently taking low-dose aspirin for coronary artery disease. What is the appropriate management regarding the aspirin?
o: Halve the aspirin dose during the acute flare
Discontinue aspirin immediately to avoid further flares
Increase aspirin dose to achieve anti‑inflammatory effect
Continue aspirin regardless of gout severity
qs.e: The note states that low-dose aspirin should not be stopped in patients taking it for specific indications like coronary artery disease, regardless of the severity of the gout, even though it can trigger flares.

qs.q: Why is the administration of aspirin strictly contraindicated in children suffering from chickenpox (varicella)?
o: Neutralization of acyclovir efficacy
Triggering of fulminant Reye's syndrome
Promotion of secondary bacterial superinfection
Exacerbation of post-herpetic neuralgia
qs.e: Salicylate use during primary varicella infection can trigger fulminant encephalitis known as Reye's syndrome, making aspirin use dangerous in children with chickenpox. Antivirals and antibiotics do not mediate this specific fatal syndrome.

qs.q: An 18-year-old male complains of severe night pain in his right thigh, which is remarkably well relieved by taking aspirin. Radiography reveals a small radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense reactive sclerotic bone in the femoral cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Osteoid osteoma
Osteoblastoma
Osteosarcoma
Ewing's sarcoma
qs.e: Osteoid osteoma is characterized by a small nidus (<2 cm) in the cortex of long bones and night pain that is classically relieved by aspirin. Osteoblastoma features a larger nidus and pain that is not relieved by aspirin.

qs.q: A 22-year-old male presents with persistent back pain that is not relieved by aspirin. Imaging reveals an expansile lytic lesion with a nidus greater than 2 cm located in the posterior elements of his vertebral column. What is the diagnosis?
o: Osteoid osteoma
Giant cell tumor
Osteoblastoma
Chondrosarcoma
qs.e: Osteoblastoma typically affects the posterior elements of the vertebral column and has a nidus greater than 2 cm with pain not relieved by aspirin. Osteoid osteoma has a smaller nidus and pain that is relieved by NSAIDs.
qs.s: Bone & Cartilage Tumors: Osteoma to Osteosarcoma Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A 16-year-old patient complains of severe bone pain in the proximal tibia that occurs predominantly at night and is dramatically relieved by aspirin. A small lesion under 2 cm is identified. What is the primary reason this tumour responds so well to aspirin?
o: The tumor lacks the calcification typically seen in osteoblastomas
The tumor produces prostaglandins that aspirin effectively inhibits
The tumor shows a t(11;22) translocation that NSAIDs block
The tumor carries a GNAS mutation leading to increased osteoclast activity
qs.e: Osteoid osteomas produce prostaglandins, which cause severe night pain and are effectively blocked by aspirin. Larger osteoblastomas do not share this dramatic pain relief response to aspirin despite being in the same tumour family.

es.q: A sputum sample from a patient with severe asthma is examined. a) Identify two characteristic microscopic findings that may be present. (2 marks) b) State the key mediator responsible for eosinophil activation in asthma. (1 mark) c) Explain the mechanism by which aspirin can induce asthma. (2 marks)
es.m: a) Two characteristic microscopic findings in asthma sputum are Curschmann Spirals and Charcot-Leyden Crystals. b) IL-5 is the key mediator for eosinophil activation in asthma. c) Aspirin-induced asthma occurs due to COX inhibition, which shifts arachidonic acid metabolism towards leukotriene production.
